title: CapisciAMe recognizes recorded words from a woman with aphasia and dysarthria in a laboratory study
summary: CapisciAMe recognized 72.65% of 936 test utterances. Twelve rehabilitation professionals averaged 56.75% on a separate listening task; spontaneous communication was not tested.
account: A 34-year-old right-handed woman took part in a single-case proof of concept at the University of Messina and IRCCS Centro Neurolesi Bonino-Pulejo. It appears in Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences (2026). She has right hemiparesis, global aphasia and dysarthria from a massive left-hemisphere hemorrhage at age 19. A compact convolutional neural network in CapisciAMe used recordings from her and 69 other Italian speakers with dysarthria. She supplied 1,120 utterances of 13 target words. The methods describe 21,947 training and 1,162 validation utterances, with her November 2022 recordings held out for testing. Utterances from November 2022 (day not given, so 1 November is used) were the held-out test set. The tailored recognizer identified 680 of 936 test utterances (72.65%). Twelve rehabilitation professionals averaged 56.75% on a separate open-response listening task with 26 recordings each. No real-world communication use is documented.
purpose: Recognize the impaired speech of a person with aphasia and dysarthria so a communication aid can voice her intended words
system: CapisciAMe speaker-dependent ASR (compact convolutional neural network, cnn-trad-fpool3) in a voice-input voice-output communication aid
model_version: cnn-trad-fpool3, trained with recordings from the participant and 69 other Italian speakers with dysarthria
developer: University of Messina and IRCCS Centro Neurolesi Bonino-Pulejo research team (CapisciAMe app developed in Italy as a research tool)
segment: Adults with post-stroke aphasia and dysarthria
taxonomy_note: The recognizer is a communication aid for a woman with dysarthria, but only a laboratory accuracy result is documented.

ratings.reason: The result is a recognition-accuracy capability measured in test sessions. The paper documents no use of the system for the patient's real communication.
Single-case proof of concept with a 13-word vocabulary.

ai_role.statement: The CNN classified the participant’s utterances within a 13-word vocabulary. Its 72.65% result and the listeners’ 56.75% mean came from different test formats and sample sizes. Training included other speakers, and spontaneous communication was not evaluated.

fields.account: A 34-year-old right-handed woman took part in a single-case proof of concept at the University of Messina and IRCCS Centro Neurolesi Bonino-Pulejo. It appears in Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences (2026). She has right hemiparesis, global aphasia and dysarthria from a massive left-hemisphere hemorrhage at age 19. A compact convolutional neural network in CapisciAMe used recordings from her and 69 other Italian speakers with dysarthria. She supplied 1,120 utterances of 13 target words. The methods describe 21,947 training and 1,162 validation utterances, with her November 2022 recordings held out for testing. Utterances from November 2022 (day not given, so 1 November is used) were the held-out test set. The tailored recognizer identified 680 of 936 test utterances (72.65%). Twelve rehabilitation professionals averaged 56.75% on a separate open-response listening task with 26 recordings each. No real-world communication use is documented.
